title: Psalm 90: Teach Us to Number Our Days
summary: The psalm sets the eternal God, who was before the mountains and has been his people's dwelling place in every generation, against the brevity of human life, which springs up like grass in the morning and withers by evening. It links human frailty with God's anger at sin and asks him to teach his people to number their days and gain a heart of wisdom. It ends by asking God to return, to satisfy them with his loving devotion, and to establish the work of their hands.
story: Psalm 90 opens Book IV of the Psalter (Psalms 90 to 106), and its position matters. Book III ended with Psalm 89's anguished question about the collapse of David's throne. Book IV answers by going back behind David to Moses, the only psalm attributed to him, and behind the monarchy to God himself: "Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations". Kings rise and fall; God was Israel's home in the wilderness before they had a king or a land, and he remains their home in the ruins. Book IV goes on to proclaim repeatedly that the LORD reigns (Psalms 93 and 95 to 99) and ends with psalms that retell the history of Israel from Egypt to exile. Psalm 90 sets the tone: a humbled people turning to the everlasting God.
historical: The heading reads "A prayer of Moses the man of God", a title given to Moses in Deuteronomy 33:1 and Joshua 14:6. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have taken it as a genuine prayer of Moses, and they note how well it fits the wilderness years, when a whole generation died in the desert under God's judgment after refusing to enter the land (Numbers 14:26-35). The psalm's language of God's anger, human life consumed, and a plea for God to return and have compassion (verse 13) echoes Moses' intercession in Exodus 32:12, where he asks God to turn from his fierce anger and relent. Many modern scholars think the psalm was written much later, perhaps during or after the exile, and was placed under Moses' name to set the response to Psalm 89's crisis under the authority of Israel's founding prophet. On that view the heading is an editorial choice, not a note of authorship. The psalm itself names no event, and both views read it as the voice of a community humbled under God's judgment.
cultural:
Ancient Israel measured time by the natural day, from evening to evening, and the night was divided into watches kept by guards on the city walls (three in the Old Testament period). A watch of the night passed unnoticed by those asleep, which is the force of verse 4: a thousand years are as brief to God as a few hours to a sleeper. Grass in the land of Israel grows quickly after the rains and withers just as quickly when the hot, dry east wind blows, so the image of grass that springs up in the morning and fades by evening was drawn from daily experience.

The span of seventy or eighty years in verse 10 was not an average life expectancy, which in the ancient world was much lower because so many died in childhood, but the full measure of a long life for those who survived. The psalm treats even that as brief. Dust (verse 3) recalls Genesis 3:19, where God tells Adam that he is dust and will return to dust. For a first reader, the psalm placed every human life, however long, inside the story of Eden and the fall.
literary: Psalm 90 is a communal lament with strong wisdom features. It moves in three stages. Verses 1 and 2 confess God's eternity. Verses 3 to 12 meditate on human brevity and its cause, God's anger at sin, and end with the prayer "So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom" (verse 12). Verses 13 to 17 turn to petition. The Hebrew verb shuv, to return or turn, links the parts: God returns people to dust in verse 3, saying "Return", and in verse 13 the people ask God himself to return. Images of time run throughout: generations, a thousand years, a day, a watch of the night, morning and evening, seventy and eighty years. The morning that brings withering grass in verses 5 and 6 becomes, in verse 14, the morning when God satisfies his people with love. The psalm ends by repeating its last request: "establish the work of our hands".

outline.t: The everlasting God, our dwelling place
Human life: dust, a watch of the night, fading grass
Consumed by God's wrath against sin
Teach us to number our days
Return, satisfy us, and establish our work

doctrines.note: God is eternal, "from everlasting to everlasting" (verse 2), existing before the mountains and the world. Time does not measure him as it measures us, and that is why he can be a dwelling place for every generation.

The psalm ties human mortality and trouble to God's response to sin: our secret sins are in the light of his presence, and our days decline under his fury. It echoes Genesis 3, where death enters the human story through sin.
Wisdom begins with an honest reckoning of how short life is and before whom it is lived. Numbering our days is not despair but a way of learning to live well.

words.note: Maon, dwelling place or habitation. Elsewhere it can describe a lair of animals or God's holy dwelling in heaven. In verse 1 God himself is the dwelling place of his people, a striking claim for a people who had lived in tents in the wilderness and would later lose their land and temple.

Manah, to count or number. In verse 12 the people ask God to teach them to count their days. The point is not arithmetic but perspective: to reckon honestly with life's limits so as to live it wisely before God.

Chokmah, wisdom. In the Old Testament wisdom is practical skill in living rightly before God, not merely knowledge. Verse 12 connects it with an awareness of mortality: a heart of wisdom is one that knows its days are numbered and lives accordingly.

christ: The New Testament applies verse 4 to the question of why Christ's return seems delayed: with the Lord one day is like a thousand years and a thousand years like one day (2 Peter 3:8), so God's patience should not be mistaken for slowness. More broadly, the psalm's problem is death under God's judgment, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one who entered that condition and overcame it. Hebrews says he tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9), and Paul teaches that as death came through Adam, resurrection comes through Christ (1 Corinthians 15:21-22). The psalm's closing prayer, that God would establish the work of our hands, finds an echo in Paul's words at the end of his chapter on resurrection, that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). These links are thematic rather than predictive. The psalm asks how brief, sinful lives can have lasting worth, and the gospel answers with the eternal God who became mortal and rose.

hard.q: Did Moses write this psalm, and does verse 10 mean God set human life at seventy years?
hard.a:
On authorship, the heading ascribes the psalm to Moses, and traditional interpreters take it as his, pointing to its fit with the wilderness generation and its echoes of Moses' language in Exodus and Deuteronomy. Many critical scholars regard it as later, noting its placement at the head of Book IV as a response to the crisis of Psalm 89 and its closeness to the concerns of exilic and later literature. Others take a middle view, that it preserves Mosaic tradition shaped for later use. Faithful readers differ on this, and the psalm's message does not depend on settling it.

On verse 10, the psalm is describing the ordinary upper range of a human life, not issuing a rule. Moses himself is said to have died at 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7), and the psalm does not contradict that; it observes that even a long life passes quickly. Verse 10 is poetry of lament, and reading it as a divine limit on lifespan misreads its genre.

questions: Verse 12 asks God to teach us to number our days. How would your week look different if you lived with a clear sense of how brief life is?
The psalm calls God our dwelling place in every generation. What does it mean to have your home in God rather than in a place, a nation, or an institution?
The psalm ends asking God to establish the work of our hands. What work of yours do you most want to last, and how does it relate to God's work?
